title: Copenhagen in 3 days: harbour, castles and Tivoli
author: Brogan
intro: Three days is enough to see the best of Copenhagen: one day for Nyhavn, the canals and the palaces, one for Rosenborg, the Round Tower and Tivoli, and one for a day trip to Louisiana, Kronborg or Malmö. Here's how to fit it together.
seo_title: Copenhagen in 3 days: a day-by-day plan (2026)
seo_description: Day 1 Nyhavn and the canals, day 2 Rosenborg, the Round Tower and Tivoli, day 3 Louisiana, Kronborg or Malmö. A realistic 3-day Copenhagen plan.

sections.heading: The short answer
sections.text:
- **Day 1:** Nyhavn, canals, palaces
- **Day 2:** Rosenborg and Tivoli
- **Day 3:** a day trip by train
- **Airport to centre:** about 15 mins

Copenhagen is compact, flat and easy on foot or by bike, so you won't spend much of your three days getting around. It's an expensive city, so plan your spending as well as your sights.

sections.heading: Three days at a glance
sections.text:
| Day | Morning | Afternoon | Evening |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Nyhavn and a canal boat | Christiansborg and the old town | Dinner by the harbour |
| 2 | Rosenborg Castle | Round Tower, Torvehallerne | Tivoli Gardens |
| 3 | Louisiana or Kronborg | Back by train | Christianshavn |

If Tivoli is closed when you visit, swap in an evening at a harbour bath in summer, or the street food and bars of the old meatpacking district.

sections.heading: Day 1: Nyhavn, the canals and the palaces
sections.text:
Start at **Nyhavn**, the canal lined with brightly painted townhouses that's on every postcard of the city. Go early, before the café terraces fill up, then take a **canal boat tour** from Nyhavn or Gammel Strand. In about an hour, it shows you the harbour, the Opera House and the Little Mermaid from the water, which saves a lot of walking.

In the afternoon, cross to **Christiansborg Palace**, home to the Danish parliament. Its tower is the tallest in the city and free to climb, with one of the best views of the old town's spires. From there, wander the old streets around Strøget and Gråbrødretorv.

Tip: the Little Mermaid statue is much smaller than people expect, and crowded by coach groups at midday. Seeing it from the canal boat is often enough.

sections.heading: Day 2: Rosenborg, the Round Tower and Tivoli
sections.text:
**Rosenborg Castle** is a Renaissance palace in the King's Garden, with the Danish crown jewels in its basement treasury. Allow an hour or two. Nearby, **Torvehallerne** is a covered food market, good for lunch, from smørrebrød (open sandwiches) to coffee and pastries. Then walk on to the **Round Tower** (Rundetaarn), a 17th-century observatory with a wide spiral ramp instead of stairs, and views over the rooftops.

Spend the evening at **Tivoli Gardens**, the 1843 pleasure garden in the middle of the city, with rides, lights and restaurants. It opens in seasons: summer, Halloween and Christmas, when the Christmas season runs from 13 November 2026 to 3 January 2027. Our post on [Tivoli Gardens at Christmas](/blog/tivoli-gardens-at-christmas) has more.

sections.heading: Day 3: a day trip by train
sections.text:
Copenhagen's trains make an easy day out, and three are worth choosing between:

- **Louisiana Museum of Modern Art**, at Humlebæk, about 35 minutes north. World-class art in a building that opens on to gardens and the sea.
- **Kronborg Castle**, at Helsingør, about 45 minutes north. The castle Shakespeare used for Hamlet, with views across to Sweden.
- **Malmö**, in Sweden, about 35 minutes over the Øresund Bridge. A relaxed old town. Take your passport, as there can be ID checks at the border.

Back in Copenhagen, finish in **Christianshavn**, with its canals and houseboats, and the free town of **Christiania** next door. Respect the signs asking visitors not to take photos in parts of Christiania.

sections.heading: Getting there and around
sections.text:
- **Flights:** about 1 hour 45 minutes from London, with direct flights from many UK airports.
- **From the airport:** the metro and the train both reach the centre in about 15 minutes, every few minutes.
- **Getting around:** walk, take the metro, or rent a bike. Cycling is how locals get about, on wide, separate lanes.
- **The Copenhagen Card:** covers public transport and entry to many sights and museums. It's worth working out whether it pays off for your plans.
- **Money:** Denmark uses the Danish krone, and cards are accepted almost everywhere. Some places don't take cash at all.

Copenhagen is one hour ahead of the UK.

sections.heading: When to go
sections.text:
- **May to August:** long light evenings, harbour swimming and Tivoli's summer season. The busiest time.
- **Mid-November to early January:** Tivoli's Christmas season and the city's Christmas markets, with short, cold days.
- **January to March:** cold, dark and quiet, but cheaper.

Our [Copenhagen guide](/destinations/copenhagen) has the month-by-month weather.

sections.heading: If you have longer
sections.text:
With a fourth day, add the other day trip from day 3, or take the train across the bridge for a night in Malmö. For a longer Scandinavian trip, [Stockholm](/destinations/stockholm), [Gothenburg](/destinations/gothenburg) and [Oslo](/destinations/oslo) are all reachable by train or a short flight.

Comparing city breaks? Our list of the [best places for a 3-day city break](/blog/best-places-for-a-3-day-city-break-in-europe) and the [city breaks](/destinations/city-breaks) page have more ideas. If you can't decide, add a few cities to somewhere.party and let the draw choose.

faqs.question: Is 3 days enough for Copenhagen?
faqs.answer: Yes. Three days covers Nyhavn, the canals, Rosenborg, the Round Tower and Tivoli, plus one day trip to Louisiana, Kronborg or Malmö.

faqs.question: When is Tivoli Gardens open?
faqs.answer: Tivoli opens in seasons: summer, Halloween and Christmas. The Christmas season runs from 13 November 2026 to 3 January 2027. Check Tivoli's website for exact dates.

faqs.question: How do you get from Copenhagen Airport to the city centre?
faqs.answer: The metro and the train both take about 15 minutes, with frequent services.

faqs.question: Is the Copenhagen Card worth it?
faqs.answer: It can be if you plan to see several paid sights and use public transport a lot. Add up your plans before buying.
